The '''inertia matrix''' $\overline{I}$ is a 3X3 matrice that describes how a rigid body’s mass is distributed relative to a chosen origin. 

It relates the body’s angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ to its angular momentum $\vec{L}$:

$$
\vec{L} = \overline{I}\vec{\omega}
$$

== Definition in orthonormal basis ==

In a orthonormal basis (Cartesian coordinate system) $B$ with origin at point $O$, and position vector $\vec{r}_m=(x,y,z)$ of each mass element $dm$, the inertia matrix of an object or system $(S)$ is

{{#content:Q2052}}

It can also be written as:

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B
=
\int_S \left[(\vec{r}_m\cdot\vec{r}_m)\,\mathbf{1}-\vec{r}_m\otimes\vec{r}_m\right]dm
$$

where $\vec{r}_m=(x,y,z)$ is always the position vector of $dm$, the $\mathbf{1}$ is the 3x3 identity matrix, and $\otimes$ denotes the [[outer product]].

=== Derivation ===

If the mass element $dm \in S$ at point $M$ rotates about $O$ with angular velocity $\vec{w}$, then its linear velocity 

$$
\vec{v}(M)=\vec{w}\wedge\vec{r}.
$$

Its angular momentum about $O$ $\vec{L}_O$ satisfies

$$
\vec{L}_O
=
\int_S \vec{r}\wedge\vec{v}(M)\,dm
=
\int_S \vec{r}\wedge(\vec{w}\wedge\vec{r})\,dm.
$$

Since

$$
\vec{r}\wedge(\vec{w}\wedge\vec{r})
=
(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{r})\vec{w}
-
(\vec{r}\cdot\vec{w})\vec{r}
$$

Writing $\vec{r}=(x,y,z)$ and $\vec{w}=(w_x,w_y,w_z)$,

$$
\vec{r}\wedge(\vec{w}\wedge\vec{r})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
(y^2+z^2)u_x-xyu_y-xzu_z\\
-xyu_x+(x^2+z^2)u_y-yzu_z\\
-xzu_x-yzu_y+(x^2+y^2)u_z
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Integrating over the solid gives

$$
\int_S \vec{r}\wedge(\vec{w}\wedge\vec{r})\,dm
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_S(y^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S xy\,dm & -\int_S xz\,dm\\
-\int_S xy\,dm & \int_S(x^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm\\
-\int_S xz\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm & \int_S(x^2+y^2)\,dm
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
w_x\\
w_y\\
w_z
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Hence

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B\cdot\vec{w}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_S(y^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S xy\,dm & -\int_S xz\,dm\\
-\int_S xy\,dm & \int_S(x^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm\\
-\int_S xz\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm & \int_S(x^2+y^2)\,dm
\end{bmatrix}
\vec{w}
$$

By definition, the inertia matrix $\overline{I}(O,S)_B$ satisfies that

$$
\vec{L}_O=\overline{I}(O,S)_B\vec{w}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\int_S(y^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S xy\,dm & -\int_S xz\,dm\\
-\int_S xy\,dm & \int_S(x^2+z^2)\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm\\
-\int_S xz\,dm & -\int_S yz\,dm & \int_S(x^2+y^2)\,dm
\end{bmatrix}
$$

== Principal basis of inertia ==

$\forall O, \exists$ orthonormal basis $B \Rightarrow$

$$
\overline{I}_O(S)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
I_{xx} & 0 & 0\\
0 & I_{yy} & 0\\
0 & 0 & I_{zz}
\end{pmatrix}$
$$

$I_{xx},I_{yy},I_{zz}$ are then known as the principal moments of inertia for $(S)$ according to $O$.

== Change of origin ==

$\forall$ orthonormal basis $B$ defined by orthonormal vectors $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, if the centre of inertia of $(S)$ is at $C$, and $\overrightarrow{OC}=(a,b,c)$, then

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B
=
\overline{I}(C,S)_B
+
\begin{bmatrix}
m(b^2+c^2) & -mab & -mac \\
-mab & m(a^2+c^2) & -mbc \\
-mac & -mbc & m(a^2+b^2)
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
$$

=== Derivation ===

For any angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$,

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B\vec{\omega}
=
\vec L(O,S)_B \\
=
\int_S \overrightarrow{OM}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OM})\,dm
$$

Since

$$
\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{CM},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overline{I}(O,S)_B\vec{\omega}
={}&
\int_S \overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})\,dm
+\int_S \overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{CM})\,dm \\
&+\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})\,dm
+\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{CM})\,dm
={}&
\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})\int_S dm
+\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge\left(\vec{\omega}\wedge\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\,dm\right) \\
&+\left(\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\,dm\right)\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})
+\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{CM})\,dm
\end{aligned}
$$

Note $\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{CM})\,dm=\vec{L}(C,S)_B = \overline{I}(C,S)_B\vec{\omega}$,

Because $C$ is the centre of inertia,

$$
\int_S \overrightarrow{CM}\,dm=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B\vec{\omega}
=
\overline{I}(C,S)_B\vec{\omega}
+
m\,\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC}).
$$

To calculate $\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})$, use the vector triple product identity:

$$
\vec{a}\wedge(\vec{b}\wedge\vec{c})
=
\vec{b}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})
-\vec{c}(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}).
$$

Taking

$$
\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{OC},\qquad
\vec{b}=\vec{\omega},\qquad
\vec{c}=\overrightarrow{OC}, \\
\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})
=
\vec{\omega}(\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\overrightarrow{OC})
-\overrightarrow{OC}(\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\vec{\omega}) \\
\because \overrightarrow{OC}=a e_1+b e_2+c e_3,\qquad \vec{\omega}=\omega_x e_1+\omega_y e_2+\omega_z e_3, \\
\therefore \overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\overrightarrow{OC}=a^2+b^2+c^2
$$

Hence

$$
\vec{\omega}(\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\overrightarrow{OC})
=
\begin{bmatrix}
a^2+b^2+c^2 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & a^2+b^2+c^2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & a^2+b^2+c^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_x\\
\omega_y\\
\omega_z
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
$$

Also,

$$
\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\vec{\omega}
=
(a e_1+b e_2+c e_3)\cdot(\omega_x e_1+\omega_y e_2+\omega_z e_3)
=
a\omega_x+b\omega_y+c\omega_z.
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{OC}(\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\vec{\omega})
&=
(a e_1+b e_2+c e_3)(a\omega_x+b\omega_y+c\omega_z) \\
&=
a(a\omega_x+b\omega_y+c\omega_z)e_1
+b(a\omega_x+b\omega_y+c\omega_z)e_2
+c(a\omega_x+b\omega_y+c\omega_z)e_3 \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
a^2 & ab & ac \\
ab & b^2 & bc \\
ac & bc & c^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_x\\
\omega_y\\
\omega_z
\end{bmatrix}_{B}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{OC}\wedge(\vec{\omega}\wedge\overrightarrow{OC})
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
a^2+b^2+c^2 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & a^2+b^2+c^2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & a^2+b^2+c^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_x\\
\omega_y\\
\omega_z
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
-
\begin{bmatrix}
a^2 & ab & ac \\
ab & b^2 & bc \\
ac & bc & c^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_x\\
\omega_y\\
\omega_z
\end{bmatrix}_{B} \\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
b^2+c^2 & -ab & -ac \\
-ab & a^2+c^2 & -bc \\
-ac & -bc & a^2+b^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\begin{bmatrix}
\omega_x\\
\omega_y\\
\omega_z
\end{bmatrix}_{B}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B\vec{\omega}
=
\overline{I}(C,S)_B\vec{\omega}
+
m
\begin{bmatrix}
b^2+c^2 & -ab & -ac \\
-ab & a^2+c^2 & -bc \\
-ac & -bc & a^2+b^2
\end{bmatrix}_{B}
\vec{\omega}
$$

Divide both sides by $\vec{\omega}$ and multiply $m$ into the matrix,

$$
\overline{I}(O,S)_B
=
\overline{I}(C,S)_B
+
\begin{bmatrix}
m(b^2+c^2) & -mab & -mac \\
-mab & m(a^2+c^2) & -mbc \\
-mac & -mbc & m(a^2+b^2)
\end{bmatrix}_{B}.
$$
